profiles.name: Mike Sturdevant
profiles.description:
Menominee Warrior Society leader who, with his brothers, led the 1975 armed occupation of the abandoned Alexian Brothers novitiate at Gresham, Wisconsin to reclaim Menominee land. Sentenced to six years in prison for his role in the 34-day takeover. Documented in PFOC Breakthrough magazine.

Michael Sturdevant was a member of the Menominee Warrior Society and one of the leaders prosecuted after its 1975 takeover of the Alexian Brothers Novitiate. Nicknamed "the General," he led the occupation. The Wisconsin Supreme Court affirmed his conviction for aiding and abetting burglary (Sturdevant v. State, 1977), rejecting his argument that the state lacked jurisdiction to try an enrolled Menominee; he was sentenced to eight years and was one of only three of the charged leaders to serve prison time. He had earlier been a federal defendant from the 1973 Wounded Knee occupation and was acquitted in that case. Born around 1944, he later worked as a Menominee tribal tax commissioner and a reporter for the Menominee Tribal News, and died in 2005. In the early hours of January 1, 1975, members of the Menominee Warrior Society — an armed group of younger Menominee men inspired by the American Indian Movement's actions at Alcatraz and Wounded Knee — seized the vacant Alexian Brothers Novitiate, a former Catholic monastery near Gresham, Wisconsin. Coming barely a year after the Menominee Restoration Act reversed the tribe's 1950s "termination," they demanded the unused estate be deeded to the impoverished tribe for use as a hospital or school, citing treaty and reversion rights. The 34-day standoff drew some 800–2,200 Wisconsin National Guard troops (deployed by Governor Patrick Lucey, who refused to order an assault) and the support of actor Marlon Brando, who called the occupiers "prisoners of war." About 39 Warriors surrendered on February 3, 1975 after the Alexian Brothers agreed to transfer the property for $1; the tribe never gained lasting possession of it.
profiles.finding: Menominee leader confirmed by 2005 obituary; tribal annual reports and Oneida newspaper remain portrait leads. Newberg school and Seymour namesakes rejected.

profiles.name: James Edward Garrett
profiles.description: James Edward Garrett was a 25-year-old Black man arrested by Marshall County, Mississippi deputies on a 1975 armed-robbery charge who was found dead in his cell (hands and feet bound) on Jan. 21, 1978; officials ruled suicide, but the United League of Marshall County disputed it and demanded a federal probe. The Black Panther Vol. 18 no.7 (1978).
profiles.finding: 1978 Marshall County jail death confirmed in Washington Post; unrelated Oregon case and Maryland veteran rejected. No portrait verified.

profiles.name: Ormistan Spencer
profiles.description: Ormistan “Tony” Spencer was a Trinidad-born production manager whose family faced repeated racist violence after buying a home in Rosedale, Queens. Their house was firebombed and then pipe-bombed. On August 27, 1975 a white crowd gathered outside after people in a passing vehicle threw garbage and bottles at the home. Spencer came outside armed for protection; when an officer grabbed the pistol it discharged and wounded Spencer and his wife. Police arrested Spencer and charged him with assault, reckless endangerment, menacing and weapon possession. In April 1976 the Queens district attorney moved to dismiss the prosecution in the interest of justice, citing the racist campaign against the family, and the court granted the dismissal. No overnight jail or prison term has been established.
profiles.finding: Rosedale attack documentary and archival blog remain leads; subject-specific frame identification required.

profiles.name: Stanton Story
profiles.description:
Stanton Story was a Black man from Pittsburgh who spent nearly five decades in Pennsylvania prisons after being convicted of the July 3, 1974 killing of Pittsburgh police officer Patrick J. Wallace Jr., and who maintained until his death that he was innocent and had been framed. According to the prosecution, Story — who had escaped from Western Penitentiary about a month earlier — shot Wallace during a street encounter; Story insisted he was not the gunman. Tried before an all-white jury, he was convicted and sentenced to death.

The Pennsylvania Supreme Court twice set aside his death sentence amid intense scrutiny of racial bias in capital sentencing (Commonwealth v. Story, 476 Pa. 391 (1978)), and on December 28, 1981 it upheld the conviction but reduced his sentence to life imprisonment. Over more than forty years inside, Story came to be recognized by prison-rights advocates as a political prisoner and a symbol of racially biased capital prosecution, and he never stopped asserting his innocence. Terminally ill with cancer, he was granted compassionate release from the State Correctional Institution at Frackville in April 2023 and died on June 9, 2023, at the age of 70.
profiles.finding: Compassionate-release and Pittsburgh case histories match; petition image remains unverified. Stanton Gill rejected.

profiles.name: Johnny Ross
profiles.description: Black youth sentenced to death at age 16 for rape in Louisiana; The Black Panther Vol. 17 no.14 (1977) reports his death sentence was reduced to 20 years after the U.S. Supreme Court struck down the death penalty for rape, with Southern Poverty Law Center attorneys pursuing a new trial.
profiles.finding: Amistad archive identifies Johnny Ross and Angola photograph; website explicitly requires reproduction permission. No permission established.

profiles.name: Milton Eugene Lindsey
profiles.description: Milton Eugene Lindsey was a 23-year-old Black worker, husband and father of two in Chattanooga, Tennessee. Early on July 21, 1974, police officers Paul O'Rear and Buddy Hullander entered a Black nightclub on Main Street without cause, demanded identification, and arrested him; one officer told the other, per Lindsey, to stop in an alley and beat him, which they did with pistols, blackjacks, boots and spit, leaving multiple lacerations to his head and back. Officers then charged him with public drunkenness and assault and battery on police officers. At trial the defense produced a Polaroid of an officer with a swollen eye alleging Lindsey had assaulted him, but witnesses — including the officers themselves — testified Lindsey was not drunk, was never given a drunk test, and was not staggering; the judge dismissed the drunkenness charge yet still handed down suspended sentences on two counts of assault and battery and a 92-dollar fine. Reconstructed from The Black Panther, Vol. XII No. 3 (August 10, 1974).
profiles.finding: 1974 Black Panther issue documents Chattanooga case; scan needs image inspection.

profiles.name: Terry Phillips
profiles.description: White Panther Party member convicted with Tom Stevens and sentenced to 5½ years-to-life over the July 1974 police raid on the party's San Francisco food-program office; The Black Panther Vol. 14 (1975) reports a 5,000-signature petition demanded an appeal bond.
profiles.finding: White Panther case found in Gay Crusader and Workers Vanguard; journalist and voice actor namesakes rejected.

profiles.name: Tom Stevens
profiles.description: White Panther Party member sentenced to 5½ years-to-life for assault with a deadly weapon after firing warning shots during a July 1974 San Francisco police raid on the party's Page Street food-program office (which police then set afire); The Black Panther Vol. 14 (1975) reports he was denied bail pending appeal in what supporters called a trumped-up prosecution.
profiles.finding: White Panther case found with Terry Phillips; actor, musician and politician namesakes rejected.

profiles.name: Sarah Bad Heart Bull
profiles.description:
Mother of a slain Sioux youth who was choked and beaten by a state trooper when she was denied entry to the 1973 Custer, S.D. courthouse; The Black Panther Vol. 14 no.27 (1976) reports she was sentenced to one-to-three years and served six months while her son's white killer got probation. 

On November 15, 1974, she was released on parole from the South Dakota Women's Prison in Yankton, where she had been confined since June 1 — her release coming as acquittals mounted in the Wounded Knee-related trials, whose dismissals and acquittals then totaled 44 (The Black Panther, December 14, 1974).
profiles.finding: Smithsonian Folkways liner notes contain captioned assault photo lead; clean recognizable crop not verified. Actress portrayal rejected.

profiles.name: Charles Beasley
profiles.description: Charles Beasley was one of the eleven Atmore-Holman Brothers — Alabama prisoners and active members of Inmates for Action (IFA) chosen from an original lot of 45 inmates to face murder and rioting charges stemming from the January 18, 1974 rebellion at Atmore prison, which began as a peaceful demonstration. On June 11, 1974 the presiding judge postponed the trial to September after carloads of supporters streamed into Brewton for the Brothers. Reconstructed from The Black Panther, Vol. XII No. 3 (August 10, 1974); his individual disposition has not been located.
profiles.finding: Atmore case in Black Panther June 1975; basketball player rejected.

profiles.name: Frank X. Moore
profiles.description: Atmore prisoner indicted in the 1974 Atmore-Holman rebellion who was 'found hanging' in the Escambia County jail before his 1975 trial; a fellow prisoner swore officials had planned his death. Deceased. The Black Panther Vol. 19 no.3 (1979).
profiles.finding: Atmore case corroborated in movement publications; portrait not verified.

profiles.name: Grover McCorvey

profiles.name: Oscar Gamba Johnson
profiles.description:
One of the Atmore-Holman Brothers (IFA), sentenced to 50 years in the framed prosecution over the 1974 Atmore-Holman prison rebellion. The Black Panther Vol. 19 no.3,10,11 (1979). 

Chairman of the Alabama prison group Inmates For Action (IFA), repeatedly retried on charges arising from a January 1974 Atmore protest against beatings and segregation; The Black Panther Vol. 14 no.9 (1975) reports he sought to move his trial to federal court, arguing the state violated his rights by denying him William Kunstler as counsel.
profiles.finding: Atmore IFA identity supported by jurists report and Freedom Archives; portrait not verified.

profiles.name: Cal Ray Biggins
profiles.description: Cal Ray Biggins was an 18-year-old Black Dallas youth indicted by the Dallas County grand jury for the January 7, 1974 murder of an elderly couple in their store. He was arrested four days later after a 5,000-dollar reward was offered and a paid informer called police to implicate him. The Black Panther reported the case as a frame-up; more than fifty supporters organized around his aunt, Mrs. Roberta King, with the Dallas Chapter of the Party. Reconstructed from The Black Panther, February 23, 1974; disposition not located.
profiles.finding: UNT Texas news script and 1974 newspaper match Dallas case; no portrait verified.

profiles.name: Joseph Remiro
profiles.description:
Vietnam War veteran and Symbionese Liberation Army member convicted with Russell Little of the November 6, 1973 assassination of Oakland Schools Superintendent Marcus Foster. Sentenced to life in 1975, he has remained incarcerated; Little's conviction was overturned but Remiro's was not. He is among the longest-held political prisoners in California.

Raised in a devout Catholic family in San Francisco, served two tours in Vietnam with the 101st Airborne before being radicalized. Founding member of the SLA in 1973 and, with Russell Little, assassinated Oakland school superintendent Marcus Foster on November 6, 1973. Arrested January 10, 1974 in Concord, California; convicted of first-degree murder and sentenced to life on June 27, 1975. His conviction stood on appeal and he was held at Pelican Bay State Prison; denied parole repeatedly through the 1980s, 1990s and 2000s before being paroled circa 2018.
profiles.finding: Captioned 1975 press photograph with Russell Little found; original provenance, subject position and rights require verification.

profiles.name: Willie Burnett
profiles.description: Black Kentucky man convicted in 1974 and sentenced to life without parole for the rape of a white woman he says he did not commit; The Black Panther Vol. 14 no.9 (1975) reports the state appeals court overturned the conviction for insufficient evidence and freed him on bond, and that he refused to plea-bargain.
profiles.finding: Kentucky case in Panther November 1975; football player and unlinked obituaries rejected.

profiles.name: Richard Dean Bucklin
profiles.description: Richard Dean Bucklin was a U.S. Army war resister who left his unit in Germany and lived in Sweden before returning to face military prosecution. Contemporary amnesty reports document his imprisonment at Fort Leavenworth.
profiles.finding: VVAW account matches draft-resister identity; no portrait verified.

profiles.name: Peter Matusewitch
profiles.description: Peter Matusewitch was a draft counselor and nonviolence trainer with the Quaker Project on Community Conflict. He was imprisoned for refusing to register with Selective Service.
profiles.finding: Quaker sources match; family-history group image lead needs identity continuity and crop verification.

profiles.name: Elliott White Haskins
profiles.description: Elliott White Haskins was a twenty-five-year-old man whom authorities alleged was associated with the Black Liberation Army. Police arrested him on October 3, 1973 during a raid at 79 Menahan Street in Bushwick, Brooklyn, where they also arrested fugitive Henry “Sha Sha” Brown. Haskins was wanted on a Freeport, Long Island, murder charge dating to February 4, 1972, and the Brooklyn district attorney said the men arrested with Brown would be charged with harboring a fugitive and hindering prosecution. Later court records, a release date and a confirmed period of confinement have not been located.
profiles.finding: Exact-name searches did not yield a verified portrait for Brooklyn BLA case.

profiles.name: Timothy Adams
profiles.description: Timothy Adams, born March 22, 1948 in Bennettsville, South Carolina, was alleged to be a member of the Black Liberation Army. Police arrested him with Henry “Sha Sha” Brown during an October 3, 1973 raid in Bushwick, Brooklyn, while Adams was already under indictment in a 1971 attempted-murder case. A later prosecution followed a December 15, 1974 shootout with police. A contemporary Black World report states that Adams was held on Rikers Island in lieu of $50,000 bail in spring 1975 on three attempted-murder counts and a weapon charge. This confirms extended pretrial confinement, although the release date and final case disposition have not been located.
profiles.finding: Safiya Bukhari and SUNY sources identify Red; actor and Texas death-row namesake rejected; conflicting dates require caution.

profiles.name: Howard Norton Machtinger
profiles.description: Howard Norton Machtinger was born in the Bronx, graduated cum laude from Columbia in 1966 in sociology, and served as an SDS regional director in 1968. Co-author of the June 1969 Weatherman statement, Days of Rage participant. Named in the April 2, 1970 Weatherman federal indictment. Led the West Coast Weather Underground collective in San Francisco. Surrendered May 11, 1978. Charges dismissed for lack of court-ordered electronic surveillance. Earned MA from SF State; taught high school in North Carolina; directed teacher-training program at UNC Chapel Hill until his death in Durham July 24, 2024.
profiles.finding: University of Chicago apf7-00685 identifies full name and Weather Underground history; Phil Lathrop photograph 1969-02-03, copyright Chicago Maroon. Separate permission explicitly required; not deployed.

profiles.name: Ronald Carter
profiles.description: Ronald Carter was one of eight Atlanta-chapter members of the Black Panther Party arrested on November 9, 1972, when Atlanta police and federal agents — a SWAT squad and detectives from the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco and Firearms — raided the chapter's office. The stated pretext was a search for a .45-caliber pistol supposedly used to shoot a policeman on October 26; the eight were instead jailed on charges of possessing explosives, though the Party noted that no such weapon was ever found. Several of the eight were released on bail pending trial. Their arrests were reported in The Black Panther (Vol. IX No. 6, November 23, 1972).
profiles.finding: Atlanta Panther reference found; Los Angeles BLA and 1994 namesakes not conflated.

profiles.name: Mario Vasquez
profiles.description: Chicano activist associated with the Crusade for Justice in Denver, arrested following the 1973 confrontation in Denver between police and the Crusade for Justice that left activist Luis Martínez dead. profiles.finding: Crusade for Justice Denver case found; Texas, Indianapolis and Los Angeles namesakes rejected.

profiles.name: Dawud Abdur Rahman
profiles.description:
Dawud Abdur Rahman is one of the four young Sunni Muslim men known as the Williamsburg Four. On January 18, 1973 — the same day that members of the Nation of Islam murdered seven Sunni Muslims, including children, at the Washington, D.C. home of Hamaas Abdul Khaalis (the Hanafi Massacre) — Dawud, Shuaib Abdur Raheem, Yusuf A. Mussadiq, and Salih Ali Abdullah entered John and Als Sporting Goods in Bushwick, Brooklyn with the intention of acquiring weapons to defend their community. A store patron alerted the NYPD, who surrounded the store in massive force. The four attempted to surrender almost immediately but were fired on and forced back inside. The siege lasted nearly forty-eight hours. NYPD Officer Stephen Gilroy was killed in the police barrage; the defense argued the fatal shot came from police, not the defendants. The four ultimately negotiated a peaceful surrender.

They were convicted in June 1974 of Officer Gilroys murder and sentenced to twenty-five years to life. Dawud Abdur Rahman was held at the Clinton Correctional Facility in Dannemora, New York under inmate number 74-A-2616. He was released on parole in October 2017, after more than forty-four years in prison. The Jericho Movement lists him among its freed political prisoners.
profiles.finding: Jericho profile matches Williamsburg Four; downloaded HTML contains banner/social/footer images but no portrait img. Planner namesake unverified.

profiles.name: Shuaib Abdur Raheem
profiles.description:
Shuaib Abdur Raheem was the eldest of the four young Sunni Muslim men known as the Williamsburg Four. On January 18, 1973 — the same day members of the Nation of Islam murdered seven Sunni Muslims, including children, in the Washington, D.C. home of Hamaas Abdul Khaalis (the Hanafi Massacre) — he led Dawud Abdur Rahman, Yusuf A. Mussadiq, and Salih Ali Abdullah into John and Als Sporting Goods at Broadway and Melrose Street in Bushwick, Brooklyn, intending to acquire weapons to defend Sunni Muslim communities in New York from anticipated attack. A patron alerted the NYPD; the four attempted to surrender almost immediately but were fired on at the back door and forced back inside. The forty-eight-hour police siege that followed killed NYPD Officer Stephen Gilroy, who the defense and witnesses inside the store later confirmed had been shot by NYPD gunfire, not by the defendants.

The four were convicted in June 1974 of Officer Gilroys murder and sentenced to twenty-five years to life. Shuaib was granted parole in 2007 after serving 32 years; the parole grant was rescinded after a campaign by the NYPD and its supporters. He was finally released on parole on July 2, 2010, after 35 years in New York state prison.
profiles.finding: Umi Archive release-letter lead and Cary Earl Robinson alias found; recognizable portrait not verified.

profiles.name: Yusuf A. Mussadiq
profiles.description:
Yusuf A. Mussadiq was one of the four young Sunni Muslim men known as the Williamsburg Four. On January 18, 1973 he, with Shuaib Abdur Raheem, Dawud Abdur Rahman, and Salih Ali Abdullah, entered John and Als Sporting Goods at Broadway and Melrose Street in Bushwick, Brooklyn intending to acquire weapons to defend Sunni Muslim communities in New York after that days murders of seven Sunni Muslims by members of the Nation of Islam in Washington, D.C. (the Hanafi Massacre). The forty-eight-hour police siege that followed killed NYPD Officer Stephen Gilroy in police gunfire that the defense argued and inside-store witnesses later confirmed had not come from the defendants.

The four were convicted in June 1974 of Officer Gilroys murder and sentenced to twenty-five years to life. Mussadiq served twenty-five years before suffering a massive stroke that left him partially incapacitated. He was released on medical parole in 1998 and died on January 1, 2003.
profiles.finding: Panther August 1974 lead and alias found; unrelated Pakistan results rejected.

profiles.name: Pedro Mario Monges
profiles.description: Pedro Mario Monges, also known as Chango Caribe and Chango Monges, was associated with the Black Liberation Army in movement publications and the Margaret Walker Center’s archival description of his prison correspondence. He pleaded guilty to federal bank robbery and received an eighteen-year sentence. Brooklyn jail records and a 1974 civil-rights decision document extended custody and his challenge to restrictions in administrative segregation. He was recaptured after an attempted escape on May 25, 1975. His eventual release date and later custody status remain unverified.
profiles.finding: Chango Caribe correspondence context retained; no verified portrait. Paraguayan namesakes rejected.

profiles.name: Louis Cale
profiles.description: Louis Cale, also known as Louis Moore, was a Detroit man who, with Henry D. Jackson Jr. and his half-brother Melvin Cale, carried out the November 10-11, 1972 hijacking of Southern Airways Flight 49 from Birmingham — a 29-hour odyssey in which the hijackers collected a $2 million ransom, wounded the copilot, and threatened to crash the plane into the Oak Ridge nuclear complex before landing in Havana. Moore and Jackson had a pending police-brutality suit against the Detroit police, the grievance behind the act, though it is generally treated as a ransom hijacking. Cuban courts sentenced him to 20 years, and he served about eight years in Cuban prisons before being returned to the United States in 1980, where he faced federal air-piracy prosecution and a further prison term.
profiles.finding: Southern Flight 49 sources match alias Louis Moore; no individual portrait verified.

profiles.description: Melvin C. Cale was the half-brother of Louis Cale (Louis Moore) and the third participant in the November 10-11, 1972 hijacking of Southern Airways Flight 49 from Birmingham — a 29-hour odyssey in which the hijackers collected a $2 million ransom, wounded the copilot, and threatened to crash the plane into the Oak Ridge nuclear complex before landing in Havana. Cuban courts sentenced him to 15 years, and he served about eight years in Cuban prisons before being returned to the United States in 1980, where he faced federal air-piracy prosecution and a further prison term.

profiles.name: Nathaniel Burse
profiles.description: Nathaniel Burse was a young Black man from Chicago's South Side and a member of De Mau Mau, an organization formed by Black servicemen in Vietnam to resist racism in the U.S. military. In 1972 he was among those arrested and prosecuted in a series of murders of white people in the Chicago suburbs (including a family of four in Barrington Hills and a family of three in Monee). The Black Panther (November 1972) reported the case as racist sensationalism — built without clear evidence and tied to State's Attorney Edward Hanrahan's re-election campaign — that had "convicted" the defendants in the press before trial. The prosecutions were heavily contested; several of the De Mau Mau defendants were convicted in 1973.
profiles.finding: De Mau Mau case in Panther/Pamoja and Freedom Archives; no verified individual portrait.

The prosecutions were heavily contested; several of the De Mau Mau defendants were convicted in 1973.
profiles.finding: De Mau Mau context corroborated; barrister and swimmer namesakes rejected.

profiles.name: Artie Adanandus
profiles.description: Artie Adanandus was seventeen when Richmond, California, police shot him in the back while arresting him on September 13, 1972. Adanandus, Clarence Peters and Forrest Blade had given two white hitchhikers a ride from Berkeley toward San Francisco; after the women later alleged kidnapping, police charged the three young Black men with attempted rape, kidnapping and robbery. The Black Panther described the prosecution as a racist frame-up. Adanandus was hospitalized after the shooting. The available report does not establish how long he remained under guard, whether he was booked into jail after treatment or how the case ended.
